name: Kingdom of England (with Lothian under the earls of Bamburgh)
notes: Lothian was held by the earls of Bamburgh within the English kingdom, though royal control there was weak. The western frontier follows the Offa's Dyke frontier zone schematically.

name: Kingdom of England
notes: Northern boundary after the loss of Lothian (traditionally dated to Carham, c.1018) and before William II's seizure of Carlisle in 1092. The Anglo-Scottish frontier in this period is poorly defined.

name: Kingdom of England
notes: Includes Carlisle after 1092. Western limit schematic; Anglo-Norman marcher lordships in Wales are shown separately.

name: Kingdom of England (northern counties held by Scotland)
notes: During the Anarchy David I of Scotland held Cumberland and, through his son Henry, much of Northumberland. The extent of Scottish control fluctuated.

name: Kingdom of England
notes: Northern counties returned to Henry II in 1157. The Anglo-Scottish border approximates the line later fixed by the Treaty of York (1237), using the modern boundary as a geographic convenience; Berwick and the Debatable Land changed hands. The Welsh side remains schematic.

name: Kingdom of England (including Wales)
notes: The Laws in Wales Acts (1535 and 1542) incorporated Wales into the kingdom of England; the shire boundaries they created are close to the later England–Wales boundary. From 1603 England and Scotland shared a monarch but remained separate kingdoms.

name: Commonwealth of England
notes: England was declared a Commonwealth in 1649. Scotland remained a separate kingdom (Charles II crowned at Scone, 1651) until conquered.

name: Commonwealth of England, Scotland and Ireland
notes: Scotland incorporated after its conquest (Tender of Union 1652; Ordinance of Union 1654).

name: Kingdom of England (including Wales)
notes: Restoration of the separate kingdoms under a shared monarch.

name: Kingdom of Great Britain
notes: Acts of Union (1706–07). England, Wales and Scotland are shown with faint internal divisions only.

name: United Kingdom (Great Britain)
notes: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland from 1801; of Great Britain and Northern Ireland from 1922. Only Great Britain is mapped.

name: Kingdom of Alba
notes: Core kingdom of Alba north of the Forth–Clyde line. Royal authority in the far north and west (e.g. Moray) was contested.

name: Kingdom of Alba (with Lothian)
notes: Lothian under Scottish rule after Carham (date and significance debated).

name: Kingdom of Scotland (with Cumbria)
notes: The former Cumbrian kingdom was absorbed by the Scottish kings at an uncertain date in the eleventh century; Carlisle was held by Dolfin, probably under Scottish lordship, until 1092.

name: Kingdom of Scotland
notes: After the loss of Carlisle. Galloway and Moray retained considerable autonomy.

name: Kingdom of Scotland (holding the northern English counties)
notes: David I's control of Cumberland and Northumberland (Treaty of Durham, 1139).

name: Kingdom of Scotland
notes: Northern English counties returned to Henry II in 1157; the Tweed–Solway frontier was confirmed by the Treaty of York (1237).

name: Kingdom of Scotland
notes: Royal authority asserted over Caithness by William I's campaigns (c.1196–1202); the earls of Orkney held Caithness as Scottish vassals. Hebrides still under Norway.

name: Kingdom of Scotland (with the Hebrides)
notes: Treaty of Perth (1266): Norway ceded the Hebrides. From 1336 to 1493 the Lordship of the Isles was largely autonomous under the Scottish crown. During the Wars of Independence much of southern Scotland was at times under English occupation, which is not shown as a boundary change.

name: Kingdom of Scotland
notes: Orkney (1468) and Shetland (1469) pledged to Scotland for Margaret of Denmark's dowry. Berwick finally English from 1482.

name: Kingdom of Scotland
notes: Restored as a separate kingdom sharing a monarch with England.

name: Kingdom of Strathclyde / Cumbria
notes: The extent and end date of the Cumbrian kingdom are uncertain; it was under strong Scottish influence and absorbed during the eleventh century. Shown until c.1070 as an approximation.

name: Kingdom of the Isles (Hebrides)
notes: Norse-Gaelic Hebridean kingdom under Norwegian overlordship; Somerled's descendants held the southern isles from the 1150s.

name: Earldom of Orkney and Shetland
notes: Under the Norwegian crown until pledged to Scotland in 1468 (Orkney) and 1469 (Shetland). Shown together until 1468.

name: Caithness (held by the earls of Orkney)
notes: Held by the Norse earls under contested Scottish and Norwegian overlordship.

name: Welsh kingdoms
notes: Gwynedd, Powys, Deheubarth, Morgannwg and Gwent among others; Gruffydd ap Llywelyn ruled all of Wales c.1055–63. Eastern edge follows the Offa's Dyke frontier zone schematically.

name: Welsh kingdoms
notes: Norman lords advanced into Gwent and, temporarily (c.1081–94), into Gwynedd.

name: Norman lordship in Gwent
notes: William fitz Osbern's conquests from Chepstow.

name: Native Welsh rule (Pura Wallia)
notes: Native rulers recovered and lost ground repeatedly: the Lord Rhys dominated the south-west c.1155–97, and Llywelyn ap Gruffudd's principality recognised in 1267 was larger than shown. This zone is a coarse approximation.

name: Anglo-Norman March of Wales
notes: Glamorgan, Gwent, Gower, Brycheiniog and Pembroke, conquered from c.1081–1093. Much of the zone was lost to Welsh rulers at times (e.g. 1136–37, 1160s–90s, 1257–67).

name: Principality of Llywelyn ap Gruffudd (after Aberconwy)
notes: Treaty of Aberconwy (1277) confined Llywelyn to Gwynedd west of the Conwy.

name: English Crown and allied lords in Wales
notes: The Perfeddwlad and royal lordships taken in 1277, together with Welsh lords allied to Edward I (e.g. Powys Wenwynwyn).

name: Marcher lordships
notes: South Wales marcher lordships.

name: Principality of Wales and the March (English Crown)
notes: After the conquest of 1282–83 and the Statute of Rhuddlan (1284), the Principality was ruled by the Crown and the March by marcher lords. Glyndŵr's revolt (1400–c.1409) briefly re-established native rule over much of Wales; this is not shown as a boundary change.
